screens.title: Private Data Collections
screens.subtitle: Securing Confidential Transactions on a Shared Ledger

narration.text: Welcome to a critical topic in enterprise blockchain: managing confidential information. While Hyperledger Fabric channels provide excellent isolation, sometimes, even within a single channel, certain transaction details must remain private to a subset of participants. Imagine a large consortium of car manufacturers, their suppliers, and dealerships all operating on the same blockchain channel to track vehicle lifecycles. A supplier's specific pricing agreement with one manufacturer should not be visible to other manufacturers or even other dealerships on that same channel. This is precisely the challenge that Hyperledger Fabric's Private Data Collections, or PDCs, are designed to solve. They offer a powerful mechanism to achieve granular data privacy without the overhead of creating entirely new channels for every confidential interaction. In this chapter, we'll explore how PDCs work, how to implement them, and why they are indispensable for complex multi-party business networks.

keyIdea.title: Granular Privacy
keyIdea.text: Private Data Collections enable a subset of organizations on a channel to share confidential data, keeping it private from other channel members.

Mastering these definitions is the crucial first step in implementing PDCs effectively in your Fabric network, ensuring your confidential data is handled correctly from the outset.

screens.title: Why Private Data Collections?
screens.subtitle: Granular Privacy within a Shared Channel

narration.text: Let's start by understanding the fundamental problem Private Data Collections solve. In Hyperledger Fabric, channels provide a powerful way to isolate transactions and data between different groups of organizations. However, what if you have a large channel with many participants, and only a subset of them needs to share highly confidential information? Creating a new channel for every private interaction would be cumbersome and inefficient. Consider our example of a car manufacturing consortium. All parties—manufacturers, suppliers, and dealerships—might be on one channel to track vehicle production and sales. But a specific pricing agreement between Manufacturer A and Supplier X is proprietary and should not be visible to Manufacturer B or any dealership. PDCs allow Manufacturer A and Supplier X to share this private pricing data directly, off-chain, while still leveraging the integrity and immutability of the main channel ledger for public transaction details. This capability is crucial for maintaining business confidentiality in complex, multi-party networks. Why Private Data Collections? means pdcs offer a flexible solution for selective data sharing among a subset of organizations on a single channel, avoiding channel proliferation.. In practical terms, granular privacy within a shared channel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Beyond Channels
keyIdea.text: PDCs offer a flexible solution for selective data sharing among a subset of organizations on a single channel, avoiding channel proliferation.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Why Private Data Collections?

The Confidentiality Challenge

Even within a shared Hyperledger Fabric channel, certain data needs to be restricted to a subset of participants.

Shared Channel

All participants track vehicle lifecycle on one channel.

Private Agreements

Supplier's pricing with one manufacturer should be hidden from others.

PDC as the Solution

Private Data Collections enable selective data sharing without creating new channels.

Targeted Visibility

Only authorized organizations see the actual private data.

Efficiency

Avoids creating numerous channels for every private interaction.

Key Takeaway

PDCs are essential for enterprise blockchain to manage confidential data among specific parties on a shared network, balancing privacy with ledger integrity.

narration.text: The core genius of Private Data Collections lies in their architecture, which elegantly balances confidentiality with the immutability of the blockchain. The actual private data, such as our car pricing agreement, is not stored directly on the main blockchain ledger. Instead, it resides off-chain in a private database, often referred to as a side database, which is specific to the authorized organizations. This means only the peers belonging to the organizations explicitly granted access to that collection will ever store or see the raw private data. What *does* get committed to the main blockchain ledger is a cryptographic hash of this private data. This hash acts as an immutable proof that the private data existed and was agreed upon by the participating parties, without revealing its actual content to unauthorized organizations. Even the ordering service, which is responsible for ensuring transaction order and integrity across the network, only sees the transaction proposal and this private data hash, never the private data itself. This design ensures that your sensitive information remains confidential while still benefiting from the tamper-proof and auditable nature of the blockchain.

keyIdea.title: Hash as Proof
keyIdea.text: Private data is stored off-chain in private databases, with only its cryptographic hash committed to the main ledger, ensuring confidentiality and integrity.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›PDC Architecture

The Dual Storage Model

Private Data Collections use a hybrid approach for data storage.

Private Database

Actual private data is stored off-chain on authorized peers.

Main Ledger

Only a cryptographic hash of the private data is committed.

Ensuring Confidentiality & Integrity

This design provides both data privacy and verifiable proof of existence.

Confidentiality

Unauthorized organizations cannot access the raw private data.

Integrity

The hash provides immutable proof of data existence and agreement.

Key Takeaway

PDCs store private data off-chain, with only a hash on the ledger, ensuring data privacy while maintaining blockchain integrity and auditability.

narration.text: To implement a Private Data Collection, you first need to define its characteristics. This definition is crucial and becomes part of your chaincode package. It's expressed as a JSON array of Collection Config objects, where each object specifies the rules for a particular private collection. Let's break down the key parameters within a Collection Config. The name field is simply the unique identifier for your collection. The policy defines which organizations are members of this collection and are therefore allowed to store and transact with its private data. This uses a syntax similar to endorsement policies, specifying organizations by their MSP IDs. required Peer Count sets the minimum number of peers that must endorse a transaction involving this private data for it to be considered valid, while max Peer Count specifies the maximum number of peers to which the private data should be disseminated via the gossip protocol. Finally, block To Live determines how many blocks after which the private data can be purged from the private database, offering a data retention mechanism. Understanding these parameters is essential for correctly configuring your private data collections to meet specific business and regulatory requirements.

keyIdea.title: Collection Configuration
keyIdea.text: PDCs are defined by a `CollectionConfig` object, specifying members, endorsement rules, data dissemination, and retention policies.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Defining PDCs

The `CollectionConfig` Object

A JSON array of CollectionConfig objects defines your private data collections.

Name

Unique identifier for the collection.

Policy

Defines authorized organizations (by MSP ID).

Required Peer Count

Min peers for transaction endorsement.

Max Peer Count

Max peers to disseminate private data to.

Data Retention & Endorsement

Additional parameters control data lifecycle and validation.

Block To Live

Number of blocks after which private data can be purged.

Endorsement Policy

Defines specific endorsement rules for the collection.

Key Takeaway

The CollectionConfig object is central to defining a PDC, controlling its members, endorsement requirements, and data retention policies.

narration.text: A critical component of defining your Private Data Collection is the policy field, which dictates precisely which organizations are authorized members. This policy uses a syntax familiar from general endorsement policies, typically specifying organizations by their Membership Service Provider, or MSP, IDs. For instance, a policy like OR open parenthesis 'Org1MSP. member', 'Org2MSP. member' close parenthesis means that any member from either Organization 1 or Organization 2 is authorized to interact with this private data collection. This is how you restrict access to the actual confidential information. Beyond just membership, the Collection Config can also include an endorsement Policy specifically for transactions involving this private data. This policy defines the set of peers that must endorse a transaction to be considered valid for this collection. It's important to distinguish between the collection's policy, which governs who *can* access the data, and the endorsement Policy, which governs who *must* validate transactions that modify it. Correctly configuring these policies is paramount to ensuring both data confidentiality and transaction integrity within your private data collections. Crafting Effective Collection Policies means collection policies define authorized organizations by msp id, while endorsement policies specify validation requirements for private data transactions.. In practical terms, specifying members and endorsement rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access Control
keyIdea.text: Collection policies define authorized organizations by MSP ID, while endorsement policies specify validation requirements for private data transactions.

Defining Collection Membership

The policy field specifies which organizations are authorized members.

Member Organizations

Identified by their MSP IDs, e.g., 'Org1MSP.member'.

Policy Example

OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member') allows members from either Org1 or Org2.

narration.text: Once your Private Data Collection is defined and deployed with your chaincode, interacting with it requires specific APIs. You won't use the standard stub. put State open parenthesis close parenthesis and stub. get State open parenthesis close parenthesis functions, as those are for public ledger state. Instead, for private data, you'll use stub. put Private Data open parenthesis collection Name, key, value close parenthesis to store confidential information and stub. get Private Data open parenthesis collection Name, key close parenthesis to retrieve it. The key difference here is the explicit inclusion of the collection Name parameter, which tells Fabric which private collection you're targeting. When a transaction involving private data is proposed, the private data itself is sent directly to the endorsing peers of the authorized organizations via a secure gossip protocol. These peers then validate the transaction and commit the private data to their local private databases. Only a hash of this private data is included in the transaction proposal response that eventually makes its way to the ordering service and the main ledger. This ensures that unauthorized organizations, even if they see the transaction on the public ledger, cannot retrieve the private data itself because their peers lack access to the specific private database for that collection.

keyIdea.title: Dedicated APIs
keyIdea.text: Use `stub.putPrivateData` and `stub.getPrivateData` with the collection name to interact with private data, distinct from public state APIs.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Chaincode Interaction

Public State APIs

For data visible to all organizations on the channel.

stub.putState(key, value)

Stores data on the public ledger.

stub.getState(key)

Retrieves data from the public ledger.

Private Data APIs

For data restricted to specific organizations within a collection.

stub.putPrivateData(collectionName, key, value)

Stores data in a private collection.

stub.getPrivateData(collectionName, key)

Retrieves data from a private collection.

Key Takeaway

Always use the dedicated putPrivateData and getPrivateData APIs, specifying the collection name, for interacting with private data collections.

screens.title: The Journey of Private Data
screens.subtitle: From Transaction Proposal to Ledger Commit

narration.text: Let's trace the journey of private data through a Hyperledger Fabric network. When a client application proposes a transaction that includes private data, this data is not immediately broadcast to the entire channel. Instead, it's sent directly to the endorsing peers of the organizations that are members of the specific private data collection. This direct, peer-to-peer communication happens via a secure gossip protocol, ensuring that the private data bypasses any unauthorized peers and the ordering service. The endorsing peers then validate the transaction, execute the chaincode, and if successful, commit the private data to their local private databases. Crucially, only a cryptographic hash of this private data is included in the transaction proposal response. This hash is then sent to the ordering service, which bundles it into a block along with other transaction hashes. Finally, this block, containing the private data hash but not the raw data, is committed to the main blockchain ledger across all peers on the channel. This multi-step process ensures that the private data remains confidential, while its existence and integrity are immutably recorded on the public ledger.

keyIdea.title: Secure Dissemination
keyIdea.text: Private data flows directly to authorized endorsing peers via gossip, with only its hash committed to the main ledger.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Data Flow

Private Data Transaction Flow

A step-by-step look at how private data moves through the network.

1.Client Proposal

Client sends private data to authorized endorsing peers.

2.Peer Validation & Storage

Endorsing peers validate and commit data to private DBs.

3.Hash to Ordering Service

Only a hash of private data is sent to the ordering service.

4.Block Commit

Block with private data hash is committed to the main ledger.

Key Takeaway

The private data flow ensures confidentiality by restricting raw data to authorized peers while maintaining an immutable, verifiable hash on the public ledger.

screens.title: Common Pitfall: Misconfigured Policies
screens.subtitle: The Impact of Incorrect Collection Policies

narration.text: One of the most common and impactful mistakes developers make when working with Private Data Collections is misconfiguring the collection policy. If an organization is not correctly included in a collection's policy, its peers will simply reject any transactions that attempt to write or even read data from that collection. This leads to endorsement failures, meaning the transaction cannot be successfully committed to the ledger. For example, if your asset Price Collection policy only includes Org1 and Org2, and Org3 attempts to invoke a chaincode function that calls put Private Data on this collection, Org3's peer will not endorse the transaction. It's crucial to meticulously review and test your collection policies to ensure all necessary organizations are correctly specified. A good practice is to start with a clear understanding of which organizations need access to which private data, and then translate that directly into your policy definitions. Any discrepancy here can lead to frustrating and hard-to-debug transaction failures, undermining the very purpose of your private data collection. Common Pitfall: Misconfigured Policies means incorrect collection policies lead to endorsement failures; ensure all necessary organizations are explicitly included in the policy.. In practical terms, the impact of incorrect collection policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Policy Accuracy
keyIdea.text: Incorrect collection policies lead to endorsement failures; ensure all necessary organizations are explicitly included in the policy.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Common Pitfalls

The Risk of Misconfiguration

Incorrectly defined collection policies can lead to critical transaction failures.

Endorsement Failures

Peers of unauthorized organizations will reject private data transactions.

Example Scenario

Org3 tries to write to a collection only for Org1 and Org2; transaction fails.

Best Practices for Policies

Ensure your collection policies are accurate and thoroughly tested.

Meticulous Review

Verify all required organizations are correctly specified in the policy.

Test Thoroughly

Simulate transactions from different organizations to confirm expected behavior.

Key Takeaway

Always double-check your collection policies; a misconfiguration can lead to transaction rejections and compromise data privacy.

screens.title: Beyond Access Control: Encryption & Graceful Handling
screens.subtitle: Addressing Data Security and Missing Data

narration.text: While Hyperledger Fabric's Private Data Collections provide robust access control, it's a common misconception to assume that private data is automatically encrypted at rest. Fabric ensures that only authorized peers can access the private database, but the data itself might not be encrypted within that database by default. For additional security requirements, such as compliance with specific data protection regulations, encryption at the application layer might be necessary before the data is sent to the chaincode. This adds an extra layer of protection, even if the private database itself were somehow compromised. Another crucial pitfall to avoid is not gracefully handling the absence of private data. If an organization that is not a member of a collection attempts to call stub. get Private Data open parenthesis close parenthesis for that collection, the A P I will return nil or an empty value, not an explicit error. Your chaincode must be prepared to handle this nil return gracefully, perhaps by indicating that the data is not accessible to the calling organization, rather than crashing or returning an unhandled error. This ensures a smooth user experience and robust application behavior.

keyIdea.title: Comprehensive Security
keyIdea.text: PDCs provide access control, but application-layer encryption might be needed for data at rest. Chaincode must gracefully handle `nil` returns for unauthorized `getPrivateData` calls.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Security & Handling

Data Encryption at Rest

Fabric ensures access control, but application-layer encryption may be needed.

Access Control vs. Encryption

PDCs control who sees data; encryption protects data even if storage is breached.

Application Layer

Consider encrypting sensitive data before sending it to chaincode.

Handling Missing Private Data

Chaincode must gracefully manage scenarios where private data is inaccessible.

getPrivateData Returns nil

For unauthorized organizations, the API returns nil, not an error.

Graceful Handling

Chaincode should anticipate and handle nil returns without crashing.

Key Takeaway

Supplement PDC access control with application-layer encryption for sensitive data, and always design chaincode to gracefully handle nil returns from getPrivateData for unauthorized access.

narration.text: Let's bring Private Data Collections to life with a practical scenario: an asset transfer. Imagine a chaincode designed to manage digital assets, where the asset ID and the current owner are public information, visible to everyone on the channel. However, the asset Price for a specific transfer is highly confidential and should only be known by the buyer and the seller involved in that particular transaction. This is a perfect use case for PDCs. Your chaincode would manage the public asset ID and owner using the standard stub. put State open parenthesis close parenthesis and stub. get State open parenthesis close parenthesis APIs, storing this information directly on the main ledger. For the confidential asset Price, you would define a private data collection, let's call it asset Price Collection, involving only the buyer and seller organizations. Then, within your asset transfer function, you'd use stub. put Private Data open parenthesis 'asset Price Collection', asset ID, price close parenthesis to store the confidential price and stub. get Private Data open parenthesis 'asset Price Collection', asset ID close parenthesis to retrieve it. The transaction recording the asset transfer on the public ledger would include a hash of the private price data, proving its existence and agreement without revealing the actual price to other network participants. This layered approach provides granular control over data visibility, making Fabric incredibly versatile for complex business networks with varying confidentiality needs.

keyIdea.title: Hybrid Data Model
keyIdea.text: Combine public state for general information with private data collections for confidential details, like an asset's public ID and private price.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Asset Transfer

Scenario: Public Asset, Private Price

Manage asset details with varying confidentiality requirements.

Public Data

assetID and owner are visible to all channel participants.

Private Data

assetPrice is confidential between buyer and seller.

Implementing the Solution

Leverage both public and private data APIs in your chaincode.

putState / getState

For public assetID and owner details.

putPrivateData / getPrivateData

For confidential assetPrice within a dedicated collection.

Key Takeaway

PDCs enable a hybrid data model, allowing public and private information to coexist and be managed securely within the same chaincode and channel.

screens.title: Defining `assetPriceCollection`
screens.subtitle: A Closer Look at the Collection Configuration

narration.text: Let's examine the collections. json file, which is where you formally define your private data collections. This example shows the definition for our asset Price Collection. Notice the name field, which is simply 'assetPriceCollection', used to reference this collection in your chaincode. The policy field is crucial: OR open parenthesis 'Org1MSP. member', 'Org2MSP. member' close parenthesis explicitly states that only members of Org1 or Org2 can access this private data. This is how we ensure confidentiality between the buyer and seller organizations. The required Peer Count is set to zero here, meaning no minimum number of peers is required to endorse for this specific collection, though a channel-level endorsement policy would still apply. max Peer Count is set to three, indicating that private data should be disseminated to up to three peers within the authorized organizations. block To Live is zero, meaning the data will persist indefinitely in the private database. Finally, the endorsement Policy within the collection config specifies that either Org1 or Org2 must sign transactions affecting this private data. This detailed configuration allows for precise control over who can see and validate your confidential information.

keyIdea.title: JSON Configuration
keyIdea.text: The `collections.json` file defines private data collections, specifying names, access policies, peer counts, and endorsement rules for granular control.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›collections.json

collections.json Definition

This JSON file defines the structure and access rules for your private data collections.

// collections.json example for defining a private data collection[  {    "name": "assetPriceCollection",    "policy": "OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member')",    "requiredPeerCount": 0,    "maxPeerCount": 3,    "blockToLive": 0,    "memberOnlyRead": true,    "memberOnlyWrite": true,    "endorsementPolicy": {      "identities": [        { "role": { "name": "member", "mspId": "Org1MSP" } },        { "role": { "name": "member", "mspId": "Org2MSP" } }      ],      "policy": {        "1-of": [ { "signed-by": 0 }, { "signed-by": 1 } ]      }    }  }]

Key Configuration Parameters

Understand the role of each field in controlling private data access and lifecycle.

policy

Defines which organizations are members and can access the private data.

endorsementPolicy

Specifies the required signatures for transactions affecting this collection.

Key Takeaway

The collections.json file is the blueprint for your private data collections, meticulously defining access, validation, and retention rules.

narration.text: Now, let's dive into the Go chaincode example to see how public and private data interactions are handled. First, we have the create Asset function. This function takes an asset ID, owner, and price as arguments. The asset ID and owner are considered public, so we marshal them into a Simple Asset struct and store them on the public ledger using stub. Put State open parenthesis asset ID, asset As Bytes close parenthesis. This is the standard way to manage data visible to all participants on the channel. Next, the read Asset function demonstrates how to retrieve this public information. It simply takes an asset ID, calls stub. Get State open parenthesis asset ID close parenthesis, and returns the public asset details. Notice that these functions do not involve any private data collection names. They interact directly with the main ledger's state database. This clear separation of concerns is fundamental to designing chaincode that effectively manages both public and private information, ensuring that only the necessary data is exposed to the broader network while sensitive details are handled through dedicated private mechanisms. Understanding this distinction is key to building robust and secure applications.

keyIdea.title: Public State Management
keyIdea.text: The `createAsset` and `readAsset` functions use `stub.PutState` and `stub.GetState` to manage public asset details visible to all channel participants.

Public Asset Creation & Reading

Functions for managing public data on the main ledger.

// Example chaincode snippet interacting with private datafunc (s *SmartContract) createAsset(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface, args []string) peer.Response {    if len(args) != 3 {        return shim.Error("Incorrect number of arguments. Expecting 3: assetID, owner, price.")    }    assetID := args[0]    owner := args[1]    price := args[2] // This will be stored privately    // Store public asset details    asset := SimpleAsset{ID: assetID, Owner: owner}    assetAsBytes, err := json.Marshal(asset)    if err != nil {        return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to marshal asset: %s", err.Error()))    }    err = stub.PutState(assetID, assetAsBytes)    if err != nil {        return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to put public state: %s", err.Error()))    }    // ... (private data storage omitted for this screen)    return shim.Success([]byte(fmt.Sprintf("Asset %s created with owner %s and private price.", assetID, owner)))}func (s *SmartContract) readAsset(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface, args []string) peer.Response {    if len(args) != 1 {        return shim.Error("Incorrect number of arguments. Expecting 1: assetID.")    }    assetID := args[0]    assetAsBytes, err := stub.GetState(assetID)    if err != nil {        return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Failed to read public asset: %s", err.Error()))    }    if assetAsBytes == nil {        return shim.Error(fmt.Sprintf("Public asset %s does not exist.", assetID))    }    return shim.Success(assetAsBytes)}

Key Code Highlights

Focus on the standard APIs for public state management.

stub.PutState()

Used to store public asset details like ID and Owner.

stub.GetState()

Retrieves public asset information from the main ledger.

Key Takeaway

Public data in chaincode is managed using standard PutState and GetState functions, ensuring visibility to all channel members.

narration.text: Now, let's focus on the functions that interact with our private data collection. The create Asset function, which we saw earlier, also includes a section for storing the private asset price. After storing the public asset details, it marshals the price into an Asset Price struct and then uses stub. Put Private Data open parenthesis "asset Price Collection", asset ID, private Price As Bytes close parenthesis. Notice the explicit mention of "asset Price Collection", which links this data to our defined private collection. Similarly, the read Asset Price function is designed to retrieve this confidential price. It calls stub. Get Private Data open parenthesis "asset Price Collection", asset ID close parenthesis. A critical point here is the error handling: if private Price As Bytes is nil, it means either the data doesn't exist, or more importantly, the calling organization is not a member of the asset Price Collection and therefore cannot access the private data. This demonstrates how Fabric enforces confidentiality at the chaincode level. Finally, the update Asset Price function follows a similar pattern, first checking for the public asset's existence, then using stub. Put Private Data to update the confidential price within the collection. These functions are the backbone of managing private data in your Hyperledger Fabric applications.

narration.text: As we conclude our exploration of Private Data Collections, let's recap the most important concepts. First, Private Data Collections, or PDCs, are a Hyperledger Fabric feature that allows a subset of organizations on a channel to transact with private data, keeping it confidential from other channel members. This is crucial for maintaining business privacy in complex networks. Second, the concept of Off-chain Storage is fundamental: the actual private data is stored in a private database, often called a side database, on authorized peers, not directly on the main blockchain ledger. This design ensures that sensitive information never becomes publicly visible. Third, only a Hash on Ledger is committed to the main blockchain. This cryptographic hash provides an immutable record and proof of existence for the private data without revealing its content. Together, these three concepts form the bedrock of how Fabric achieves granular data confidentiality while preserving the integrity and auditability of the blockchain.

Key Concepts to Remember

Essential Takeaways (Part 1 of 2)

Private Data Collections (PDC)

A Fabric feature enabling a subset of organizations on a channel to share confidential data, hidden from others.

Off-chain Storage

Actual private data is stored in a private database on authorized peers, not directly on the blockchain ledger.

Hash on Ledger

Only a cryptographic hash of the private data is committed to the main ledger, proving existence without revealing content.

Summary Takeaway

Private Data Collections are a cornerstone of Hyperledger Fabric's privacy model, enabling selective data confidentiality through off-chain storage and on-chain cryptographic proofs.

narration.text: Let's continue with the remaining key concepts that underpin Private Data Collections. Fourth, the Collection Policy is a JSON definition that specifies the members of a private data collection, along with endorsement requirements and data retention policies. This policy is your primary tool for controlling access to private data. Fifth, interacting with private data in chaincode requires specific APIs: Put Private Data and Get Private Data. These functions are used to store and retrieve data within a specified private data collection, distinct from the public state APIs. Finally, the Gossip Protocol plays a vital role. It's used by Fabric peers to securely disseminate private data directly to authorized peers within a collection, bypassing the ordering service and unauthorized peers. These three concepts—policy, APIs, and the gossip protocol—are essential for configuring, implementing, and understanding the secure flow of private data in your Hyperledger Fabric applications. Mastering them will enable you to build robust and confidential blockchain solutions.
